data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
The US Treasury on Friday imposed sanctions on four Iranians who served as "oil trustees".
It said they had sought to collect funds from illicit international oil sales and pass them to the Iranian government to evade earlier sanctions and a US naval blockade.
In many cases, the trustees kept the oil revenues for personal gain, the Treasury said in a statement.
Those sanctioned include Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former intelligence officer in Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Majid Taj, brother of Mehdi Taj, the president of Iran’s football federation.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
A Palestinian man was killed by Israeli forces near Ramallah on Friday as the forces carried out raids, detentions and a home demolition across the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was killed in Dura al-Qare, northeast of Ramallah, by Israeli forces who are still withholding his body, the Palestinian General Authority of Civil Affairs said.
In Jaba, south of Jenin, Israeli forces beat a man who was taken to hospital, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. A convoy of army vehicles later stormed the town and detained two young men. In nearby Qabatiya, soldiers fired on a vehicle and detained two people.
In Jericho, a young Palestinian man was shot in the foot during a raid on the al-Bayader neighbourhood.
South of Hebron, Israeli forces raided al-Fawwar refugee camp as residents left Friday prayers, firing tear gas and beating a young man who was later hospitalised.
In nearby Beit Ummar, Israeli forces stormed the town, ordered merchants to close their shops and fired barrages of tear gas and stun grenades, according to local media activist Mohammad Awad. He said soldiers severely beat and detained two men, aged 22 and 45.
In the Tulkarm governorate, several young men were detained as Israeli forces raided the town of Anabta.
Also on Friday, Israeli bulldozers demolished a home in al-Mazra’a al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah.
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers stole the contents of a roadside fruit stand south of Jenin and trees from a nursery in Jaba, surveillance footage showed.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February had been the president’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States”.
After the midterm elections, Vance blamed the war for the Republicans’ historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict.
His statement, posted on social media, was widely seen as a break with Trump as the vice president weighs a 2028 White House bid.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”
Trump said on Friday that he was not unhappy with Vance’s conclusion but that it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgement that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.
“People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion,” Trump said. “But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they’re crazy.”
Vice President JD Vance on Iran: "The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsored terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands potentially, of innocent people. The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the President of the United States."
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) November 20, 2026

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
Iran still has hope that diplomacy can end its war with the United States, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, adding that the two sides are still exchanging messages through mediators.
“We are seeking an agreement with the US that would ensure there is no further war afterwards,” Araghchi told an Iranian newspaper.
He said Tehran saw no need to change the intermediaries in the talks.
Before going any further, Iran wants guarantees that Washington is serious about negotiating, he said, and it has discussed the form and nature of possible confidence-building measures with the mediators.
Iran’s first demand is for US President Donald Trump to state explicitly that he wants an agreement, Araghchi said.
He added that it was not surprising for Trump to take a new position every day, or even to reverse what he had said the day before.
One of Iran’s red lines is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country, Araghchi stated, though he believed a fair solution could be reached.
He also said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US met Iran’s seven conditions.
His comments came hours after Trump reiterated that the US had "total control" over the strait.
Iran’s official position on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons remains the same, and its nuclear doctrine has not changed, Araghchi added.

data.author: Sean Mathews

Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on

Sulaymaniyah is reeling from the economic toll of the Iran war and grappling with an emboldened regional power next door
A market in the city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq's Kurdistan Region is said to be the largest bazaar in the region, on 11 November 2026 (Sean Mathews/MEE)
Off
If US President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business.
The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through Iran first.
“The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye.
Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. In addition to a naval blockade, the US is pressing countries like Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan to seal their borders with Iran. Earlier this month, the US announced a task force to blockade trade across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Baran has no political beef with the US. On the contrary, he says, “George W. Bush overthrew Saddam Hussein. He helped Kurdistan. I don’t prefer Iran to the US,” he said over a glass of anise-flavoured Arak and hookahs at a restaurant in Sulaymaniyah.
“But this war has not been good for business or our economy.”
Baran is a microcosm of the city he calls home.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza, civil defence says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza, civil defence says
Israeli strikes killed six people in the Gaza Strip on Friday, the civil defence agency in the war-shattered territory told AFP, despite a ceasefire.
Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, said that four Palestinians were killed and several others wounded in an Israeli airstrike southwest of Bureij refugee camp in the central Gaza Strip on Friday.
The civil defence also said one Palestinian was killed in an Israeli drone strike targeting a tent in the Al-Munasara camp for displaced people in Deir al-Balah.
Another person was killed in a drone strike north of Nuseirat refugee camp, also in the central Gaza Strip.
The Israeli military told AFP it had "targeted multiple military operatives" in several strikes, which came a day after the army said it had completed a ground incursion in the central Gaza Strip.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Trump: 'ICC out of control, can't go in and arrest heads of countries'
US President Donald Trump has said the International Criminal Court was "out of control", while claiming China "agreed for the first time to condemn the abuses and overreach" of the court, AFP reported.
Trump, on his return from a summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, complained that the ICC believes "they can go in and arrest the heads of countries, and they can't do that. They can do it for no reason -- so we condemned that as a group."
Washington has vowed to dismantle the court, which it targeted with new sanctions last month. Trump has been angered by the tribunal's move to issue an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza genocide.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Several Palestinians injured in attacks by Israeli settlers, forces in West Bank
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Several Palestinians injured in attacks by Israeli settlers, forces in West Bank
Several Palestinians were injured in a wave of attacks by Israeli settlers and military across the occupied West Bank, according to reports by the Palestinian news agency, Wafa, and Al Jazeera.
* The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its crew treated a Palestinian man who was beaten by Israeli forces in the town of Jaba', south of Jenin.
*Israeli soldiers opened fire at a vehicle in the Qabatiya town, south of Jenin, and detained two inhabitants.
* Ahmed Kawazbeh, head of Al-Maniya village council, southeast of Bethlehem, tells Wafa that a group of Israeli settlers raided the home of Mohammad Khalil Jabareen early Thursday morning and attacked his family members with batons and pepper spray. Jabareen's son, Raafat, and his wife sustained bruises and injuries and suffered from suffocation while attempting to protect their children. They were taken to Beit Jala Governmental Hospital for treatment.
The attackers also smashed the family’s vehicle. Kawazbeh said this was the second time the family had been targeted in a settler attack.
*Israeli forces arrested at least 17 Palestinians, including former prisoners, in raids across the occupied West Bank. About 20 others were detained in Tubas and Tammun, where soldiers turned a house into a military post, according to Al Jazeera.
*Israeli settlers shot and wounded a Palestinian olive picker in Nabi Saleh, northwest of Ramallah, and assaulted others harvesting olives in Berin, east of Hebron.
*Israeli forces demolished a Palestinian home in al-Mazraa al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah, and prevented residents of Khirbet Samra in the northern Jordan Valley from repairing tents damaged by heavy rain, according to Al Jazeera.
*Footage released by Israeli rights group, Mistaclim, shows a group of Israeli settlers stealing fruit and vegetables from a roadside vendor during an incursion into the village of Al Fundukumiya, in Jenin.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UKMTO weekly report says six vessels attacked in and around Hormuz
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
UKMTO weekly report says six vessels attacked in and around Hormuz
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said six attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in the past week, while shipping traffic remained about 65 percent below pre-war levels.
In its weekly report published on Friday, UKMTO said four of the six incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and two in the Arabian Gulf.
The UKMTO recorded 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits during the seven days to November 18, including US-facilitated movements. The combined figure was down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound the previous week.
Around half of Strait of Hormuz transits involved energy carriers. Most vessels broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route, although UKMTO noted an increase in traffic along the southern route.
No attacks were recorded in the past week in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandab, with the last confirmed attack recorded on August 24. However, vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb remain about 22 percent below levels existing before 22 July when Houthis announced a blockade.

UNDP official: 'Gaza's suffering must compel us to ask difficult questions'
A top United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) official has said the suffering endured by people in Gaza "must compel us to ask difficult questions".
“What strikes you immediately is the scale of the destruction in Gaza, where more than 90% of the population depends on humanitarian assistance. The contrast between what we consider normal—food, water and quality of life—and the suffering endured by people in Gaza must compel us to ask difficult questions,” Haoliang Xu, Under-Secretary-General and Associate Administrator, UNDP, said.
Xu said a defining feature of our time is "polycrisis, with challenges that extend far beyond any one place", according to a post on X by MED Dialogues.
"The conflict in the Middle East, for example, is costing countries across the region at least 3.6% of GDP, with some UNDP estimates reaching 6%,” Xu said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says
Calls on the Israeli authorities to protect Palestinian olive farmers and ensure they can reach their groves safely have not been acted upon, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said, citing the Humanitarian Country Team.
Instead, in the first nine months of 2026, Israeli authorities uprooted or otherwise damaged more than 10,000 Palestinian-owned trees and saplings across the West Bank, mostly olives, the statement adds.
The Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which brings together UN bodies and humanitarian NGOs, said more than 400 Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest since September have resulted in casualties or damage to property, including to more than 4,000 trees and saplings.
The number of attacks this year exceeds that recorded in any previous olive harvest season. This year’s harvesting window is closing, the team said, but there is still some time to act.
"Humanitarian NGOs and UN agencies urge the Israeli authorities in the strongest possible terms: end all attacks on Palestinians and their livelihoods, as required by international law. Ensure farmers have free, safe, sufficient and reliable access to their land. The team added that perpetrators must be stopped and held to account," the statement read.

Gaza Board of Peace says it will hand keys to UN if Israel fails to honour commitments
A senior adviser to the Trump-appointed Gaza Peace Council has warned that the body could return responsibility for the enclave to the United Nations if Israel does not honour its commitments under the 20-point plan, Israeli outlet Ynet has reported.
Josh Gruenbaum, who was appointed to the council by Trump and previously worked in the White House, told Ynet: “We have been extremely patient and have given Israel its space. But it is frustrating that now with the elections behind us — even if they haven’t resulted in a clear coalition — that Israel is failing to move forward on the commitments Netanyahu made to President Trump.”
“If this political leadership says it no longer wants to honour what they committed to, just let us know,” Gruenbaum said “And we will throw the keys back to the UN.”
Ynet said it had seen a presentation prepared by council members, who visited Israel last week. Its final slide, titled “Other alternatives to Gaza”, reportedly lists several scenarios if the plan is abandoned.
These include a future US administration and Congress ordering a different reconstruction plan, the UN Security Council taking over “perhaps through UNRWA”, the Palestinian Authority and Hamas.
The last scenario, according to the slide, is that Israel becomes fully responsible for the administrative and humanitarian costs of Gaza’s population.
Another slide reportedly says Hamas formally accepted the plan in July, pledging to give up its weapons and transfer governmental powers to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body meant to run the territory.
“We are at a standstill due to political elements within the Netanyahu government who have prevented us from progressing and from testing whether Hamas will keep its word,” Gruenbaum said, according to Ynet.
Gruenbaum also criticises Israel for failing to allow sufficient aid into Gaza before winter

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rights group calls for ban on white phosphorus, cites Israel's use in Gaza
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Rights group calls for ban on white phosphorus, cites Israel's use in Gaza
Cairo-based rights group, Maat for Peace, Development and Human Rights, has called for an explicit ban on the use of white phosphours, which has repeatedly been used by Israel in Gaza and southern Lebanon, Al Jazeera reported.
White phosphorus can cause severe burns, ignite repeatedly and produce intense heat and toxic smoke.
Human rights groups and The New York Times said in June they have documented Israel's use of the chemical white phosphorus over civilian areas in Lebanon.
White phosphorus is not banned under international law, but it is illegal to use the chemical in and near populated areas since it can cause widespread harm. Israel has been accused by the international human rights community for decades of using the substance in a way that puts civilians in danger.
In a working paper submitted at the review session for the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the group said the current treaty has glaring gaps that allow for the use of white phosphorus.
Following an impasse after talks started on Monday, the conference ran over time and ended early on Saturday, with states agreeing to continue talks aimed at developing measures on lethal autonomous weapons by 2028.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Cycle of conflicts must end': Leaders and experts call for cooperation on Middle East conflicts
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
'Cycle of conflicts must end': Leaders and experts call for cooperation on Middle East conflicts
Regional and international leaders and experts called for dialogue and cooperation to promote stability in the Middle East at the 12th edition of the MED – Mediterranean Dialogues, held in Naples from November 19 to 21.
Promoted by Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation and the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), the conference brought together regional and international leaders to discuss Middle East conflicts, security cooperation, maritime threats and prospects for regional stability.
MED Dialogues shared on X key remarks by speakers on Middle East-related issues.
*Dialogue is essential. The security of any country depends on the stability of its neighbourhood, including Iran. We need to create space for mutual security guarantees—not to end one conflict only for another cycle to begin, but to build an interdependent security arrangement that respects the interests of all. ( Manal Radwan, Advisor and Special Envoy to the Saudi Foreign Minister for Negotiations and Peace Efforts, Saudi Arabia )
*The Mecca Agreement is not an alternative to Turkey’s existing alliances, but a complementary one. Turkey joined it to reinforce deterrence and build upon the capabilities of the three countries involved. It does not name anyone in the region as an enemy and allows other regional powers to be part of it. (Çağrı Erhan, Chief Advisor to the Turkish President)
*Geography shapes maritime security challenges, but addressing them is a shared responsibility. Securing the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf is not only the responsibility of the countries along their shores: it requires the entire international community, because trade through these routes serves the whole world. (Walid A. Al-Khuraiji, Saudi Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs)
*We need to be at the table whenever Yemen’s future is discussed. Decisions about our country cannot be made
